conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that the best available evidence does not support the claim that induced abortion increases breast cancer risk, pointing out methodological flaws in older studies and citing large prospective studies that show no increased risk.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion:** The best available evidence in the supplied results does **not** support the claim that induced abortion increases breast-cancer risk.

Why the claim arose: older research, largely case–control studies relying on women’s later reports of prior abortions, sometimes found a small positive association. A 1996 meta-analysis concluded induced abortion was an independent risk factor, though this is an observational finding and cannot by itself establish causation. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8944853/

The key methodological issue is **reporting/recall bias**: after diagnosis, women with breast cancer may be more likely to disclose a previous induced abortion than women without cancer. The large 2004 collaborative reanalysis (53 studies; about 83,000 breast-cancer cases) found that retrospective and prospective results differed substantially. In studies with abortion information recorded prospectively—before any cancer diagnosis—the relative risk for induced abortion was 0.93, i.e., no increased risk. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140673604158352

Later systematic review/meta-analysis work based on prospective studies likewise did not support a positive association. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10552-015-0536-1

The American Cancer Society summarizes the current evidence as indicating that abortion does not influence breast-cancer risk. https://www.cancer.org/cancer/risk-prevention/medical-treatments/abortion-and-breast-cancer-risk.html
